stem.en: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃C–OH is:

explanation.en: The longest chain containing the C–OH carbon has three carbons; C-2 carries the OH and a methyl group: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol).

stem.en: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?

explanation.en: In propan-2-ol the carbon carrying –OH is bonded to two other carbons, so it is secondary. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary; propan-1-ol is primary.

stem.en: The C–O bond in phenol (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm) because:

options.en: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character
Oxygen in phenol is sp³ hybridised

explanation.en: The oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring by resonance, and the carbon is sp² hybridised. Both shorten the C–O bond.

stem.en: The C–O–C bond angle in methoxymethane is 111.7°, a little more than the tetrahedral angle. This is due to:

options.en: Repulsion between the two bulky alkyl groups

explanation.en: The two methyl groups are bulkier than hydrogen atoms and repel each other, opening the angle slightly beyond 109.5°.

solution.en: The two methyl groups are bulkier than hydrogen atoms and repel each other, opening the angle slightly beyond 109.5°.

stem.en: Benzene-1,3-diol is commonly called:

explanation.en: Benzene-1,2-diol is catechol, benzene-1,3-diol is resorcinol and benzene-1,4-diol is quinol (hydroquinone). Cresols are methylphenols.

stem.en: Hydroboration–oxidation of propene (B₂H₆, then H₂O₂/OH⁻) gives:

explanation.en: Boron adds to the less substituted carbon, and is then replaced by –OH: the net result is anti-Markovnikov addition of water, giving propan-1-ol.

stem.en: Reduction of a ketone with NaBH₄ gives:

explanation.en: R₂C=O + 2[H] → R₂CH–OH. The carbonyl carbon already carries two R groups, so the alcohol is secondary.

stem.en: In the manufacture of phenol from cumene, the by-product is:

explanation.en: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which with dilute acid splits into phenol and acetone.

stem.en: CH₃MgBr reacts with ethanal, and the product is hydrolysed. The alcohol formed is:

explanation.en: CH₃⁻ from the Grignard adds to the carbonyl carbon of CH₃CHO, giving (CH₃)₂CH–OMgBr; hydrolysis gives (CH₃)₂CHOH, propan-2-ol. Aldehydes other than HCHO give 2° alcohols.

solution.en: CH₃⁻ from the Grignard adds to the carbonyl carbon of CH₃CHO, giving (CH₃)₂CH–OMgBr; hydrolysis gives (CH₃)₂CHOH, propan-2-ol.
Aldehydes other than HCHO give 2° alcohols.

stem.en: Which Grignard reagent and carbonyl compound give 2-methylbutan-2-ol after hydrolysis?

explanation.en: C₂H₅MgBr + (CH₃)₂C=O → (CH₃)₂C(OMgBr)C₂H₅ → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃, 2-methylbutan-2-ol. The others give butan-2-ol, ethanol and butan-2-ol respectively.

stem.en: Which of these compounds of similar molar mass has the highest boiling point?

explanation.en: Ethanol molecules are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds (b.p. 351 K). Methoxymethane, propane and chloroethane cannot hydrogen-bond with themselves.

stem.en: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:

options.en: The ethoxide ion is stabilised by the +I effect
The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance

explanation.en: The negative charge of phenoxide is delocalised over the ring. Ethoxide has no such resonance and the ethyl group (+I) even pushes more electron density onto its oxygen, destabilising it.

stem.en: Which of the following reacts with aqueous NaOH?

explanation.en: Phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is acidic enough to react with NaOH, forming sodium phenoxide. Alcohols are weaker acids than water and do not react with NaOH; ethers are not acidic.

stem.en: The strongest acid among the following is:

explanation.en: Each nitro group at ortho or para withdraws electrons and stabilises the phenoxide ion. Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, pKa ≈ 0.7) is about as strong as many mineral acids.

solution.en: Each nitro group at ortho or para withdraws electrons and stabilises the phenoxide ion.
Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, pKa ≈ 0.7) is about as strong as many mineral acids.

stem.en: The correct order of acid strength is:

explanation.en: pKa values: p-nitrophenol ≈ 7.1, phenol ≈ 10.0, p-cresol ≈ 10.2, ethanol ≈ 15.9. –NO₂ (electron-withdrawing) raises acidity; –CH₃ (electron-donating) lowers it; alcohols are far weaker than phenols.

stem.en: Lucas reagent is:

explanation.en: Lucas reagent (conc. HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂) converts alcohols to insoluble alkyl chlorides: turbidity at once for 3°, in a few minutes for 2°, and not at room temperature for 1°.

stem.en: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give:

explanation.en: In polar water, phenol ionises partly and the ring becomes very strongly activated; all three ortho and para positions are brominated, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

stem.en: Sodium phenoxide heated with CO₂ under pressure, followed by acidification, gives:

explanation.en: This is Kolbe’s reaction: the phenoxide ion is attacked by CO₂ at the ortho position, giving 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid).

stem.en: Phenol treated with chloroform and aqueous NaOH, then acidified, gives:

explanation.en: Reimer–Tiemann reaction: dichlorocarbene from CHCl₃/NaOH attacks the ortho position; hydrolysis gives a –CHO group, so the product is salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).

solution.en: Reimer–Tiemann reaction: dichlorocarbene from CHCl₃/NaOH attacks the ortho position; hydrolysis gives a –CHO group, so the product is salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).

stem.en: o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile but p-nitrophenol is not, because:

options.en: p-Nitrophenol has a lower molar mass

explanation.en: In the ortho isomer the –OH and –NO₂ are close enough to hydrogen-bond within one molecule, so molecules do not associate. The para isomer forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds and is far less volatile.

stem.en: Williamson synthesis of ethers uses:

options.en: An alkyl halide and a sodium alkoxide
An aldehyde and a Grignard reagent

explanation.en: R–X + R′–O⁻Na⁺ → R–O–R′ + NaX: an SN2 reaction of an alkoxide ion with an alkyl halide.

stem.en: Ethers boil at much lower temperatures than isomeric alcohols because:

options.en: Ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond with one another

explanation.en: Ethers have no O–H hydrogen, so there is no intermolecular hydrogen bonding; methoxyethane boils near pentane, far below propan-1-ol.

stem.en: Anisole (methoxybenzene) is heated with HI. The products are:

explanation.en: The O–CH₃ bond breaks (SN2 at the methyl carbon); the O–aryl bond has partial double-bond character and does not break. So phenol and CH₃I form.

stem.en: The best Williamson route to tert-butyl methyl ether, (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃, is:

options.en: (CH₃)₃C–OH + CH₃OH with conc. H₂SO₄ at 413 K

explanation.en: A tertiary halide with a strong base (CH₃O⁻) undergoes elimination, giving 2-methylpropene. Using the tertiary alkoxide with the primary (methyl) halide lets SN2 proceed.

solution.en: A tertiary halide with a strong base (CH₃O⁻) undergoes elimination, giving 2-methylpropene.
Using the tertiary alkoxide with the primary (methyl) halide lets SN2 proceed.

stem.en: Ethanol heated with conc. H₂SO₄ at 413 K gives mainly:

explanation.en: At 413 K, one ethanol molecule attacks the protonated form of another (SN2), giving ethoxyethane. At 443 K elimination wins and ethene forms.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): Phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
Reason (R): The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge over the benzene ring, while the ethoxide ion is not.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Resonance stabilisation of phenoxide favours ionisation of phenol; ethoxide has no such stabilisation (and the ethyl group's +I effect destabilises it). R explains A.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): o-Nitrophenol is more volatile (steam volatile) than p-nitrophenol.
Reason (R): o-Nitrophenol molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, so its molecules are not associated and it is more volatile. p-Nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonding. A is true; R is false.

passage.en: A lab assistant finds three unlabelled bottles, X, Y and Z, each containing one of the isomeric alcohols butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. She adds Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂) to a few drops of each at room temperature. X turns cloudy immediately, Y turns cloudy after about five minutes, and Z stays clear.

stem.en: Which alcohol is in bottle X?

options.en: It cannot be decided from this test

explanation.en: Lucas reagent reacts through a carbocation; tertiary alcohols react at once (immediate turbidity), secondary in a few minutes, primary not at room temperature. X is the tertiary alcohol.

passage.en: A lab assistant finds three unlabelled bottles, X, Y and Z, each containing one of the isomeric alcohols butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. She adds Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂) to a few drops of each at room temperature. X turns cloudy immediately, Y turns cloudy after about five minutes, and Z stays clear.

stem.en: When the alcohol in bottle Z is oxidised with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC), the product is:

explanation.en: Z gives no turbidity, so it is the primary alcohol butan-1-ol. PCC oxidises a primary alcohol only to the aldehyde: butanal.

stem.en: Which of the following statements are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.en: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance
p-Nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol
p-Cresol is more acidic than phenol
Ethanol reacts with aqueous NaOH to form sodium ethoxide to a large extent

explanation.en: Phenoxide spreads its charge over the ring; ethoxide cannot. The –R, –I nitro group stabilises the phenoxide further, so p-nitrophenol (pKa 7.1) is stronger. The electron-releasing CH₃ of p-cresol destabilises the anion, making it weaker than phenol. Ethanol (pKa about 16) is weaker than water, so NaOH hardly converts it to ethoxide.

stem.en: Which of the following statements are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.en: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol gives turbidity with the Lucas reagent almost at once
Phenol with bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol
A tertiary alcohol is oxidised by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to a ketone with the same number of carbons
Sodium phenoxide heated with CO₂ under pressure, then acidified, gives salicylic acid

explanation.en: Tertiary alcohols form a stable carbocation, so the Lucas test is immediate. The –OH group activates the ring so strongly that bromine water substitutes all ortho and para positions. A tertiary alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon and resists mild oxidation. Kolbe’s reaction gives 2-hydroxybenzoic (salicylic) acid.

stem.en: The pKa of phenol is 10.0. Calculate the pH of a 0.1 M aqueous solution of phenol (assume the degree of ionisation is small). Give the answer to two decimal places.

explanation.en: For a weak acid, pH = ½(pKa − log c) = ½(10.0 − log 0.1) = ½(10.0 + 1) = 5.50.

stem.en: 4.70 g of phenol is treated with excess bromine water. What mass of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (in g) is formed if the reaction is complete? (Molar masses: phenol 94 g/mol, 2,4,6-tribromophenol 331 g/mol.) Give the answer to two decimal places.

explanation.en: Moles of phenol = 4.70/94 = 0.05 mol. One mole of phenol gives one mole of tribromophenol, so mass = 0.05 × 331 = 16.55 g.

stem.en: The correct order of acid strength is:

explanation.en: pKa values: p-nitrophenol 7.1, phenol 10.0, ethanol about 15.9. The lower the pKa, the stronger the acid.

solution.en: pKa values: p-nitrophenol 7.1, phenol 10.0, ethanol about 15.9.
The lower the pKa, the stronger the acid.

stem.en: Phenol is heated with chloroform and aqueous NaOH, and the product is acidified. The main product is:

explanation.en: This is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction: a –CHO group enters the ortho position of phenol, giving 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde).

solution.en: This is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction: a –CHO group enters the ortho position of phenol, giving 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde).

stem.en: Which of these isomeric alcohols has the highest boiling point?

explanation.en: All have the same mass and can form hydrogen bonds, but branching makes the molecule more compact and lowers the surface area. The straight-chain primary alcohol, butan-1-ol (about 391 K), boils highest.

stem.en: In the cumene process, cumene hydroperoxide is treated with dilute acid. Besides phenol, the other product is:

explanation.en: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) + O₂ → cumene hydroperoxide, C₆H₅C(CH₃)₂–O–OH. Acid-catalysed rearrangement gives phenol + acetone (CH₃COCH₃). The process is valued precisely because acetone is a useful co-product.

stem.en: Propene reacts with water in the presence of dilute H₂SO₄. The major product is:

explanation.en: Acid-catalysed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end to give the more stable 2° carbocation CH₃C⁺HCH₃, which is captured by water → propan-2-ol. Propan-1-ol is the hydroboration–oxidation (anti-Markovnikov) product.

stem.en: Propene is treated with B₂H₆ followed by H₂O₂ / NaOH. The product is:

explanation.en: Hydroboration–oxidation adds the boron to the less substituted carbon; oxidation replaces B by OH with retention. Net result: anti-Markovnikov addition of water → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. No carbocation forms, so no rearrangement.

stem.en: Which alcohol gives turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂) at room temperature?

explanation.en: The Lucas test forms the alkyl chloride (insoluble → turbidity) via a carbocation. 3° alcohols (2-methylpropan-2-ol) react at once, 2° in about 5 minutes, and 1° alcohols do not react appreciably at room temperature.

stem.en: Industrially, methanol ('wood spirit') is now made by:

explanation.en: CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH over ZnO–Cr₂O₃ at 573–673 K and 200–300 atm. 'Wood spirit' refers to its old source, the destructive distillation of wood (not coal tar). Fermentation of molasses gives ethanol.

options.en: Catalytic hydrogenation of CO (CO + 2H₂) over ZnO–Cr₂O₃ at high pressure
Hydration of ethene with dilute H₂SO₄

stem.en: Phenol is shaken with excess bromine water. The white precipitate formed is:

explanation.en: In water phenol partly ionises to the strongly activating phenoxide ion, and the polar solvent helps polarise Br₂, so all ortho/para positions are brominated → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt). Mono-bromination needs a non-polar solvent (CS₂/CHCl₃) at low temperature.

stem.en: Sodium phenoxide is heated with CO₂ at about 400 K under 4–7 atm and the product is acidified. This is Kolbe's reaction and the product is:

explanation.en: Phenoxide is a strong enough nucleophile to attack the weak electrophile CO₂, mainly at the ortho position → sodium salicylate → salicylic acid on acidification. Salicylaldehyde comes from the Reimer–Tiemann reaction (CHCl₃/NaOH).

stem.en: Phenol on treatment with CHCl₃ and aqueous NaOH, followed by acidification, gives mainly:

explanation.en: Reimer–Tiemann reaction: a –CHCl₂ group is introduced ortho to –O⁻ and hydrolysed by alkali to –CHO → 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde). With CCl₄ instead of CHCl₃ the product is salicylic acid.

stem.en: Ethanol (b.p. 351 K) boils far above its isomer methoxymethane (b.p. 248 K) because:

explanation.en: Both are C₂H₆O (same molar mass). Ethanol has an O–H bond and forms intermolecular H-bonds; extra energy is needed to break them. Ethers have no O–H so their molecules cannot H-bond to each other.

options.en: Ethanol has a higher molar mass
Ethanol molecules are associated by intermolecular hydrogen bonding
Methoxymethane has a larger dipole moment

stem.en: Phenol is heated with zinc dust. The organic product is:

explanation.en: Zinc dust removes the oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO. Cyclohexanol would need catalytic hydrogenation (H₂/Ni) of the ring.

stem.en: Propan-1-ol is oxidised with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in CH₂Cl₂. The product is:

explanation.en: PCC is a mild, anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage for 1° alcohols → CH₃CH₂CHO. Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄ would go on to propanoic acid. Propanone would need a 2° alcohol (propan-2-ol).

stem.en: Ethanol is heated with conc. H₂SO₄. At 443 K the main product is X; at 413 K (with excess ethanol) it is Y. X and Y are:

explanation.en: Higher temperature favours elimination (intramolecular dehydration) → CH₂=CH₂ at 443 K. At 413 K a second ethanol molecule attacks the protonated alcohol (SN2) → C₂H₅OC₂H₅. Remember: 'higher T, alkene; lower T, ether'.

options.en: X = ethyl hydrogen sulphate, Y = ethanal

stem.en: 4.6 g of ethanol reacts with excess sodium metal. The volume of hydrogen gas evolved at STP (in litres, molar volume 22.4 L) is ____. (in L)

explanation.en: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. Moles of ethanol = 4.6/46 = 0.1 mol → H₂ = 0.05 mol → 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 L. A common slip is taking 1 mol H₂ per mol alcohol (2.24 L).

stem.en: Arrange in decreasing order of acidic strength: (I) ethanol (II) phenol (III) 4-nitrophenol (IV) 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).

explanation.en: Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised, so phenols ≫ ethanol. –NO₂ (–R, –I) at para delocalises the negative charge further → 4-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 7.1) is strongest. –CH₃ (+I, hyperconjugation) destabilises the phenoxide → p-cresol (pKa ≈ 10.2) is slightly weaker than phenol (10.0). Ethanol (pKa ≈ 15.9) is weakest.

stem.en: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃C–CH(OH)–CH₃, is heated with conc. H₂SO₄. The major alkene formed is:

explanation.en: Loss of water gives the 2° cation (CH₃)₃C–C⁺H–CH₃. A 1,2-methyl shift gives the 3° cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH(CH₃)₂. Loss of H⁺ to form the most substituted (Saytzeff) alkene gives the tetrasubstituted (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene. 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene is the product if no rearrangement occurred; 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene is the minor Hofmann-type alkene.

stem.en: The best Williamson-synthesis route to 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl methyl ether) is:

explanation.en: The alkyl halide must be methyl or 1° because the alkoxide attacks by SN2. With a 3° halide the strongly basic CH₃O⁻ causes E2 elimination → 2-methylpropene. Acid dehydration of a 3° alcohol also gives mainly the alkene, not the ether.

stem.en: 2-Methoxy-2-methylpropane is heated with one equivalent of HI. The products are:

explanation.en: After protonation, the C–O bond to the tertiary carbon breaks to give the stable (CH₃)₃C⁺ (SN1); I⁻ captures it → (CH₃)₃C–I + CH₃OH. With primary/methyl groups only (e.g. CH₃OC₂H₅) cleavage is SN2 and I⁻ attacks the smaller methyl group, giving CH₃I — that is the trap in option A.

stem.en:
Statement I: In the nitration of phenol with dilute HNO₃ at 298 K, o-nitrophenol can be separated from p-nitrophenol by steam distillation.
Statement II: o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile because of intramolecular hydrogen bonding, while p-nitrophenol is associated by intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

explanation.en: In o-nitrophenol the –OH H-bonds to the adjacent –NO₂ oxygen (chelation), so molecules are not associated with each other or with water → lower b.p., steam volatile. p-Nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds → higher b.p., not steam volatile. Statement II directly explains Statement I.

options.en: Both statements are true and II is the correct explanation of I
Both statements are true but II is not the correct explanation of I
Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true

stem.en:
Assertion (A): Alcohols react with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen.
Reason (R): Alcohols are stronger acids than water.

explanation.en: A is true: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂ (alcohols are Brønsted acids). R is false: alkyl groups (+I) destabilise the alkoxide, so alcohols are slightly weaker acids than water — alkoxides are stronger bases than OH⁻ (RO⁻ + H₂O → ROH + OH⁻).

options.en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem.en:
Match the reaction (List I) with its reagent (List II).
List I: (P) Kolbe's reaction (Q) Reimer–Tiemann reaction (R) Williamson synthesis (S) Lucas test
List II: (1) CHCl₃ + aq. NaOH (2) R–X + R′–ONa (3) conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂ (4) NaOH, CO₂ at 400 K, 4–7 atm

explanation.en: Kolbe: phenoxide + CO₂ (4). Reimer–Tiemann: CHCl₃/NaOH → dichlorocarbene (1). Williamson: alkyl halide + alkoxide (2). Lucas test: conc. HCl / ZnCl₂ (3). Swapping Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann (option B) is the usual confusion.

stem.en: Which combination will NOT give 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃, after acidic work-up?

explanation.en: The target is a 3° alcohol with groups CH₃, CH₃, C₂H₅. Acetone + EtMgBr and butanone + MeMgBr both supply these. An ester reacts with 2 equivalents of RMgX: ethyl propanoate + 2CH₃MgBr → C₂H₅C(OH)(CH₃)₂ (same product). Butanal + CH₃MgBr gives a 2° alcohol, pentan-2-ol.

stem.en: Cinnamaldehyde, C₆H₅CH=CH–CHO, is to be converted into C₆H₅CH=CH–CH₂OH. The most suitable reagent is:

explanation.en: NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the polar C=O but leaves the non-polar C=C alone → cinnamyl alcohol. H₂/Pd also reduces the C=C. Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) reduces C=O to CH₂. KMnO₄ is an oxidant.

stem.en: Ethanoic acid is esterified with ethanol labelled with ¹⁸O (C₂H₅–¹⁸OH) in the presence of conc. H₂SO₄. The ¹⁸O is found in:

explanation.en: The alcohol oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon of the acid; the –OH lost as water comes from the acid (acyl–oxygen cleavage). So the label stays in CH₃CO–¹⁸O–C₂H₅ and the water contains ordinary oxygen.

options.en: Both the ester and water equally

stem.en: Vapours of 2-methylpropan-2-ol are passed over heated copper at 573 K. The product is:

explanation.en: Cu at 573 K dehydrogenates 1° alcohols to aldehydes and 2° alcohols to ketones. A 3° alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon, so it undergoes dehydration instead → (CH₃)₂C=CH₂. This is a classic test to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.

stem.en: Which ether cannot be made in good yield by any Williamson synthesis?

explanation.en: Williamson needs at least one alkyl halide that is methyl/1° (or benzyl). For di-tert-butyl ether both partners would be 3°: (CH₃)₃C–Br + (CH₃)₃CO⁻ gives only elimination (2-methylpropene). Anisole is made from C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I; benzyl methyl ether from C₆H₅CH₂Cl + CH₃ONa.

stem.en: Anisole undergoes Friedel–Crafts acetylation (CH₃COCl / anhydrous AlCl₃). The major product is:

explanation.en: –OCH₃ activates the ring (+R) and directs ortho/para; the para product dominates for steric reasons → 4-methoxyacetophenone (with some 2-isomer). The meta product is not favoured; phenyl acetate is an O-acylation product of phenol, not anisole.

stem.en: Picric acid is best prepared from phenol by:

explanation.en: Phenol is so activated that conc. HNO₃ oxidises much of it to tarry products. Converting it first to the sulphonic acid (deactivating –SO₃H groups) and then nitrating replaces the –SO₃H groups by –NO₂ → 2,4,6-trinitrophenol in good yield. Dilute HNO₃ gives only o/p-nitrophenol.

options.en: Treatment with dilute HNO₃ at 298 K
Sulphonation with conc. H₂SO₄ followed by treatment with conc. HNO₃
Reaction with NaNO₂ / HCl at 273 K

stem.en: The correct order of acidic strength of the following in the liquid / solution phase is:

explanation.en: Each alkyl group (+I) pushes electron density onto O, destabilising the alkoxide; bulkier alkoxides are also less well solvated. So acidity falls from CH₃OH to 3° alcohols. (In the gas phase the order reverses because of polarisability — not asked at NCERT level.)

stem.en: In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction the electrophile that attacks the phenoxide ring is:

explanation.en: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from CHCl₃ to give CCl₃⁻, which loses Cl⁻ to form the neutral, electron-deficient dichlorocarbene :CCl₂. This attacks the ortho position of phenoxide; the –CHCl₂ group is then hydrolysed to –CHO. CCl₃⁻ is an intermediate, not the electrophile.

stem.en: Phenol → (i) NaOH (ii) CO₂, 400 K, 4–7 atm (iii) H⁺ → X; X + (CH₃CO)₂O / H⁺ → Y. Y is:

explanation.en: Kolbe's reaction gives salicylic acid (X). Acetic anhydride acetylates the phenolic –OH → 2-acetoxybenzoic acid, aspirin (Y). Methyl salicylate would need methanol/H⁺ (esterifying the –COOH instead).

stem.en: Phenol reacts with bromine in CS₂ at 273 K. The major product is:

explanation.en: In a non-polar solvent at low temperature phenol is not ionised and Br₂ is not strongly polarised, so only monobromination occurs at the o/p positions; the para isomer is major for steric reasons. Bromine water would give the tribromo compound.

stem.en: Which alcohol is dehydrated most readily by conc. H₂SO₄?

explanation.en: Acid dehydration of 2°/3° alcohols goes through a carbocation (E1). 2-Phenylpropan-2-ol gives a carbocation that is both tertiary and benzylic (resonance with the ring) and the alkene formed is conjugated with the ring → fastest. Order: 3° benzylic > 3° > 2° > 1°.

stem.en: The total number of structural isomers (alcohols and ethers together) with molecular formula C₄H₁₀O is ____.

explanation.en: Alcohols (4): butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Ethers (3): 1-methoxypropane, 2-methoxypropane, ethoxyethane. Total = 7 (stereoisomers not counted).

stem.en:
How many of the following give a positive iodoform test (I₂ / NaOH)?
ethanol, methanol, propan-2-ol, propan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, 1-phenylethanol, pentan-3-ol

explanation.en: The iodoform test needs CH₃CH(OH)– (oxidised by I₂/NaOH to CH₃CO–). Positive: ethanol, propan-2-ol, butan-2-ol, 1-phenylethanol = 4. Methanol and propan-1-ol lack it; tert-butanol cannot be oxidised; pentan-3-ol has ethyl groups on the carbinol carbon.

stem.en: 9.4 g of phenol is treated with excess bromine water. The mass (in g) of 2,4,6-tribromophenol formed, assuming complete conversion, is ____. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Br = 80) (in g)

explanation.en: C₆H₅OH (M = 94) → C₆H₂Br₃OH. M(tribromophenol) = 6(12) + 3(1) + 16 + 3(80) = 331 g/mol. Moles of phenol = 9.4/94 = 0.1 → product 0.1 × 331 = 33.1 g (consuming 0.3 mol Br₂).

stem.en: 0.37 g of a saturated monohydric alcohol reacts with excess CH₃MgI to liberate 112 mL of methane at STP. The molar mass of the alcohol (in g mol⁻¹) is ____.

explanation.en: ROH + CH₃MgI → CH₄ + ROMgI, 1 mol CH₄ per –OH (Zerewitinoff method). Moles CH₄ = 112/22400 = 0.005 mol = moles of alcohol. M = 0.37/0.005 = 74 g/mol → C₄H₉OH (a butanol).

stem.en: An alcohol A (C₅H₁₂O) gives turbidity with Lucas reagent in about 5 minutes and a yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH. On heating with conc. H₂SO₄ it gives an alkene whose ozonolysis yields acetone and acetaldehyde. A is:

explanation.en: Acetone + acetaldehyde come from (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃ (2-methylbut-2-ene). '5 minutes' → 2° alcohol; iodoform → CH₃CH(OH)–. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CH–CH(OH)–CH₃, fits: Saytzeff dehydration (also via hydride shift to the 3° cation) gives 2-methylbut-2-ene. Pentan-2-ol gives pent-2-ene → acetaldehyde + propanal. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is 3° (immediate turbidity, no iodoform); 3-methylbutan-1-ol is 1°.

stem.en: 2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol (neopentyl alcohol) is heated with conc. H₂SO₄. The major product is:

explanation.en: (CH₃)₃C–CH₂OH has no β-hydrogen on the quaternary carbon, so simple elimination is impossible ('2,2-dimethylpropene' cannot exist). Loss of water is assisted by a 1,2-methyl shift giving the 3° cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃, which loses H⁺ to give the more substituted 2-methylbut-2-ene (major) and some 2-methylbut-1-ene (minor).

stem.en: 1-Methylcyclohexene is treated with BH₃·THF, then H₂O₂ / NaOH. The product is:

explanation.en: B adds to the less substituted ring carbon (C-2) and H to C-1, both from the same face (syn). Oxidation replaces B by OH with retention. So the new H on C-1 and the OH on C-2 are cis, which makes the CH₃ (on C-1) and OH trans → trans-2-methylcyclohexanol (racemic). 1-Methylcyclohexanol is the Markovnikov (acid-hydration) product.

stem.en: 4-Methylphenol (p-cresol) is subjected to the Reimer–Tiemann reaction (CHCl₃, aq. NaOH, then H⁺). The major product is:

explanation.en: The para position is blocked by CH₃, so the –CHO enters ortho to –O⁻. Numbering the aldehyde as C-1: OH at C-2 and CH₃ at C-5 → 2-hydroxy-5-methylbenzaldehyde. Option A puts the CHO para to OH (impossible, CH₃ is there); option D is a carboxylic acid (CCl₄ variant).

stem.en: Arrange in decreasing order of acidity: (I) phenol (II) 2-nitrophenol (III) 3-nitrophenol (IV) 4-nitrophenol.

explanation.en: o- and p-NO₂ stabilise phenoxide by both –R and –I; m-NO₂ only by –I. So o, p > m > phenol. The ortho isomer is slightly weaker than para because intramolecular H-bonding holds the proton. pKa: 4-nitro 7.1 < 2-nitro 7.2 < 3-nitro 8.3 < phenol 10.0.

stem.en: Counting stereoisomers separately, the number of alcohols with molecular formula C₄H₁₀O is ____.

explanation.en: Structural alcohols: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (4). Only butan-2-ol has a stereocentre (C-2 bears H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅) → R and S. Total = 4 + 1 = 5.

stem.en: Periodic acid cleaves the C–C bond between adjacent carbons bearing –OH groups (one HIO₄ per C–C bond cleaved). The number of moles of HIO₄ consumed by one mole of glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is ____.

explanation.en: Glycerol HOCH₂–CH(OH)–CH₂OH has two C–C bonds, each between carbons carrying OH. Both are cleaved: 2 HIO₄ → 2 HCHO + 1 HCOOH (the middle carbon ends up as formic acid).

stem.en: Which of the following give phenol as one of the products?

explanation.en: A: acid rearrangement → phenol + acetone. B: SN2 at CH₃ → phenol + CH₃I (phenol is not converted further, because the aryl C–O bond resists substitution). C: ArN₂⁺ + H₂O → ArOH + N₂ + H⁺. D: aryl halides are inert to aqueous NaOH at room temperature — the Dow process needs NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm.

stem.en: Which statements about ethers are correct?

explanation.en: A true: autoxidation gives hydroperoxides — never distil ether to dryness. B false: the products are phenol and CH₃I. C true: the ether O accepts H-bonds from water (ethoxyethane and butan-1-ol have similar solubility, ~7–8 g per 100 mL). D false: ethers cannot H-bond with each other, so they boil much lower than isomeric alcohols.

options.en: Diethyl ether slowly forms explosive peroxides when stored in air and light
Anisole reacts with HI to give iodobenzene and methanol
The miscibility of ethers with water resembles that of alcohols of similar molar mass
Ethers boil higher than isomeric alcohols because of their dipole moment

stem.en: Which of the following are more acidic than phenol?

explanation.en: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilise phenoxide. 4-NO₂ (pKa 7.1) and 4-Cl (–I outweighs weak +R; pKa ≈ 9.4) are stronger acids than phenol (10.0). 4-CH₃ (+I) and 4-OCH₃ (+R dominates; pKa ≈ 10.2) are weaker.

stem.en: Which of the following give a tertiary alcohol (after aqueous acidic work-up where needed)?

explanation.en: A: ketone + RMgX → 3° alcohol, (CH₃)₃COH. B: ester + 2RMgX → ketone intermediate → 3° alcohol, (CH₃)₃COH. C: aldehyde (other than HCHO) + RMgX → 2° alcohol (propan-2-ol). D: Markovnikov hydration through the 3° cation → (CH₃)₃COH.
